name: Kalta Minor Minaret

localizedNames.ja: カルタ・ミノル・ミナレット

architect: Usto Qalandar Khivaki (ceramic glazing by Master Abdulla Jin)
locationInSite: West Square, immediately inside Ata-Darvoza (West Gate) beside Muhammad Amin Khan Madrasah
verifiedBy: Ichan-Qala State Historical & Architectural Museum-Reserve Archive
shortDescription: Khiva's iconic turquoise-tiled unfinished minaret, commissioned by Muhammad Amin Khan in 1851 to be the tallest tower in the Islamic world.

localizedShortDescriptions.en: Khiva's iconic turquoise-tiled unfinished minaret, commissioned by Muhammad Amin Khan in 1851 to be the tallest tower in the Islamic world.
localizedShortDescriptions.uz: 1851-yilda Muhammad Aminxon tomonidan musulmon olamidagi eng baland minora bo'lishi niyat qilib qurila boshlangan, firuza koshinlar bilan qoplangan mashhur tugallanmagan minora.
localizedShortDescriptions.ru: Знаменитый незавершённый бирюзовый минарет Хивы, заложенный Мухаммад Амин-ханом в 1851 году как самая высокая башня исламского мира.
localizedShortDescriptions.ja: 1851年にムハンマド・アミン・ハンがイスラム世界最高峰を目指して着工した、鮮やかなトルコ石タイルに覆われたヒヴァ象徴の未完ミナレット。
localizedShortDescriptions.ko: 1851년 무함마드 아민 칸이 이슬람 세계에서 가장 높은 탑으로 세우려 했던 히바의 상징적인 청록색 미완성 미나레트입니다.
localizedShortDescriptions.es: El icónico minarete inacabado de azulejos turquesa de Jiva, encargado en 1851 por Muhammad Amin Khan para ser la torre más alta del mundo islámico.

historicalFacts: Construction began in 1851 (1268 AH) under the personal decree of Khiva's ruler, Muhammad Amin Khan, right beside his monumental madrasah.

The minaret was originally intended to rise 70 to 80 meters high, which would have surpassed the Kalyan Minaret in Bukhara (46.5 meters) and become the tallest minaret in Central Asia and the Islamic world.
Construction halted abruptly in 1855 after Muhammad Amin Khan was killed in battle near Serakhs in present-day Turkmenistan.
His successor, Abdulla Khan, did not resume the costly project, leaving the tower standing at 29 meters and earning it the name 'Kalta Minor' ('Short Minaret') or 'Kok Minor' ('Blue Minaret').
Because it was never finished, it is the only minaret in Khiva whose entire exterior surface from base to rim is completely clad in glazed ceramic tiles.

The poetic Persian calligraphy encircling the upper band was composed by the celebrated Khorezmian historian and poet Muhammad Riza Agahi (1809–1874) and was carefully restored between 1996 and 1997 for Khiva's 2,500th anniversary.
architecturalDetails: The circular base has an extraordinary diameter of 14.2 meters, narrowing slightly toward the top, engineered to support a 70+ meter shaft.
Its massive brick foundation descends approximately 15 meters deep into the desert earth using wooden beams and reed cushioning layers to absorb seismic shocks.

Glazed majolica bands alternate turquoise, deep cobalt blue, white, and ochre-green geometric stars, vegetal spirals, and Nasta'liq inscriptions crafted by master tilemaker Abdulla (nicknamed 'Abdulla Jin' for his seemingly magical skill).

Originally, an arched wooden bridge connected the second floor of Muhammad Amin Khan Madrasah directly to an elevated doorway inside the minaret so the muezzin could climb its internal spiral staircase.
Even at 29 meters tall, the wall thickness at the base exceeds 3 meters of kiln-fired Khorezmian brick bound with ganch (gypsum-lime mortar).
localLegends: Legend of Seeing Bukhara: Local elders say Muhammad Amin Khan ordered the tower built so tall that he could stand at its summit and watch over the rival Emirate of Bukhara more than 400 kilometers away across the Kyzylkum Desert.

Legend of the Architect's Escape: According to Khiva folklore, the Emir of Bukhara secretly promised the master architect immense riches if he would build an even taller minaret in Bukhara after finishing Kalta Minor. Discovering this secret pact, Muhammad Amin Khan planned to execute the architect upon completion. Warned in advance, the architect fashioned wings (or vanished overnight into the desert), leaving the tower permanently unfinished.

Whisper of the Blue Glaze: Local craftsmen recall that Abdulla Jin mixed crushed desert plant ash (ishqor) and cobalt oxides under moonlight so the turquoise tiles would never fade under the harsh Khorezm sun—and indeed, after more than 170 years, the glaze still gleams brilliantly.
visualCues: Short, wide, thick cylindrical tower completely covered in bright turquoise, cyan, cobalt blue, and white glazed ceramic tiles
Flat horizontal unfinished rim at the top (no lantern cupola or pointed dome)
Horizontal bands of geometric tilework and calligraphic script bands wrapping the entire cylinder
Standing directly next to the brick facade of Muhammad Amin Khan Madrasah near the West Gate

name: Juma Mosque
architect: Patron Abdurakhman Mehtar under Avaz Inak; master Khorezmian woodcarvers across 10 centuries
locationInSite: Central Axis of Ichan-Qala along the main east-west street between Ata-Darvoza and Palvan-Darvoza
verifiedBy: Ichan-Qala State Historical & Architectural Museum-Reserve Archive
shortDescription: A rare Central Asian hypostyle Friday mosque famous for its forest of 213 hand-carved wooden columns spanning ten centuries of Khorezmian artistry.

localizedShortDescriptions.en: A rare Central Asian hypostyle Friday mosque famous for its forest of 213 hand-carved wooden columns spanning ten centuries of Khorezmian artistry.
localizedShortDescriptions.uz: O'n asrlik Xorazm yog'och o'ymakorligi san'atini o'zida jamlagan 213 ta naqshinkor ustundan iborat Markaziy Osiyodagi noyob jome masjidi.
localizedShortDescriptions.ru: Уникальная многоколонная пятничная мечеть Центральной Азии, знаменитая лесом из 213 резных деревянных колонн, охватывающих десять веков искусства Хорезма.
localizedShortDescriptions.ja: 10世紀にわたるホラズムの木彫芸術を伝える213本の彫刻木柱の森で有名な、中央アジアでも極めて珍しい多柱式金曜モスク。
localizedShortDescriptions.ko: 10세기에 걸친 호레즘 목각 예술이 담긴 213개의 수작업 나무 기둥 숲으로 유명한 중앙아시아의 희귀한 다주식 금요 모스크입니다.
localizedShortDescriptions.es: Una singular mezquita hipóstila de Asia Central famosa por su bosque de 213 columnas de madera tallada a mano que abarcan diez siglos de arte jorezmio.

historicalFacts: The earliest historical mention of a Friday mosque on this exact site appears in the 10th-century writings of Arab geographer Al-Muqaddasi.
The current single-story structure was reconstructed between 1788 and 1789 by Abdurakhman Mehtar, a wealthy Khivan statesman, during the reign of Avaz Inak.

When rebuilding the mosque, craftsmen purposefully rescued and incorporated ancient carved wooden columns salvaged from earlier ruined Khorezmian mosques and medieval cities, turning the hall into a living museum of Khorezmian woodcarving.

Out of the 213 wooden columns inside, 4 rare columns date back to the 10th–11th centuries (decorated in early floral Kufic script), 17 columns date from the 12th–15th centuries, and the rest come from the 18th–19th centuries.
An engraved marble waqf (endowment) tablet from 1788–1789 mounted near the entrance records the land revenues permanently dedicated to maintaining the mosque and its scholars.
The adjacent brick minaret stands 32.5 meters tall with a base diameter of 6.2 meters and collapsed once in the 17th century before being rebuilt alongside the 1788 restoration.
architecturalDetails: Unlike typical domed Timurid mosques with grand portals and courtyards, Juma Mosque follows an archaic Arabian-style hypostyle plan: a vast enclosed flat-roofed hall measuring 55 meters by 46 meters.
The roof rests on a grid of 213 black elm (karagach) and poplar columns arranged at intervals of roughly 3.15 meters, seated on carved stone bases to protect the timber from rising ground salinity.

No two columns have identical carvings—motifs progress from stylized 10th-century vegetal reliefs and Kufic inscriptions to intricate 18th-century Khivan floral arabesques (islimi) and stalactite muqarnas capitals.

Two large open rectangular sky-wells (light shafts) cut directly into the flat roof provide natural daylight, cool desert cross-ventilation, and a tranquil indoor courtyard feel with small garden trees.
The low wooden beam ceiling and column spacing were carefully proportioned so the imam's voice from the southern mihrab carries clearly across thousands of worshippers without microphones.
localLegends: The Singing Elm Columns: Khiva woodcarvers teach that authentic black elm (gujum) timber must be seasoned in water and shade for years before carving; elders say that in quiet early mornings, the oldest 10th-century columns faintly creak as if whispering prayers from a thousand years ago.

The Pillar of Blessing: Visitors have long sought out the oldest surviving 10th-century column near the central skylight, where the ancient Kufic floral carving has been polished smooth by centuries of reverent hands, believing it symbolizes the continuity of Khorezm across Mongol invasions and desert storms.

Natural Air-Conditioning Secret: Local residents explain that during 45°C Khiva summers, entering Juma Mosque drops the felt temperature by more than 10 degrees—the two open sky-wells act as thermal chimneys drawing cool shaded air across the thick mud-brick walls.
visualCues: Interior forest of dozens of carved dark wooden columns supporting a flat wooden-beamed ceiling
Open square skylight openings in the wooden ceiling letting diagonal shafts of sunlight hit the brick floor
Carved wooden column bases resting on stone pedestals with intricate floral and Kufic relief carvings
Plain baked-brick exterior wall with carved wooden entrance doors and a slender brick minaret rising 32.5 meters

name: Tosh-Hovli Palace
architect: Usto Nurmuhammad Tajikhan (initial phase) & Usto Qalandar Khivaki (completion); majolica by Abdulla Jin
locationInSite: Eastern sector of Ichan-Qala, just west of Palvan-Darvoza (East Gate)
verifiedBy: Ichan-Qala State Historical & Architectural Museum-Reserve Archive
shortDescription: The 'Stone Courtyard' royal palace of Allakuli Khan, renowned for its 163 labyrinthine rooms, three grand courtyards, and Khiva's most dazzling blue-and-white majolica.

localizedShortDescriptions.en: The 'Stone Courtyard' royal palace of Allakuli Khan, renowned for its 163 labyrinthine rooms, three grand courtyards, and Khiva's most dazzling blue-and-white majolica.
localizedShortDescriptions.uz: 1830–1838-yillarda Olloqulixon qurdirgan 163 xonali 'Tosh Hovli' saroyi — 3 ta ulkan hovli va Xivaning eng nafis ko'k-oq koshinlari bilan mashhur.
localizedShortDescriptions.ru: Дворец Аллакули-хана «Каменный двор» (1830–1838) со 163 комнатами, тремя парадными дворами и самой роскошной сине-белой майоликой Хивы.
localizedShortDescriptions.ja: 1830〜1838年にアッラクリ・ハンが築いた「石の中庭」宮殿。163の部屋、3つの中庭、ヒヴァ随一の青白マヨリカ装飾で知られます。
localizedShortDescriptions.ko: 1830~1838년 알라쿨리 칸이 세운 '돌의 안뜰' 궁전으로, 163개의 방과 3개의 중정, 히바 최고의 청백 마욜리카 타일로 유명합니다.
localizedShortDescriptions.es: El palacio del 'Patio de Piedra' de Allakuli Khan (1830–1838), famoso por sus 163 estancias laberínticas, tres grandes patios y la mayólica azul y blanca más deslumbrante de Jiva.

historicalFacts: Commissioned by Allakuli Khan (reigned 1825–1842) as a grander, more sumptuous royal residence than the older Kunya-Ark fortress.
Construction took eight years, from 1830 to 1838, involving over 1,000 skilled craftsmen and laborers.

The palace contains more than 163 rooms arranged around three distinct functional courtyards: the Harem (family quarters, built first in 1830–1832), the Ishrat-Hovli (ceremonial reception and banquet courtyard, 1832–1834), and the Arz-Hovli (official court of justice and petitions, 1837–1838).

In the Harem courtyard, five tall north-facing covered iwans (terraces) stood side by side: four identically proportioned iwans for the Khan's four legitimate wives, and a larger, more lavishly decorated fifth iwan reserved exclusively for the Khan.
The palace's defensive windowless exterior brick walls with corner turrets resemble a miniature fortress designed to protect the royal household from urban unrest and assassination.

After the 1920 abolition of the Khiva Khanate, Tosh-Hovli became part of the protected heritage museum complex, preserving one of the finest intact 19th-century Islamic palace interiors in Central Asia.
architecturalDetails: Every grand courtyard features circular raised baked-brick platforms (sufa) where nomadic-heritage Khivan Khans still pitched felt yurts during cold winters and formal tribal receptions.

The walls of all three courtyards are sheathed in extraordinary blue, turquoise, and white Khorezmian majolica tiles painted by Master Abdulla Jin with interlocking floral medallions and fine calligraphic friezes.
Single-column carved karagach (elm) pillars rest on sculpted marble bases inscribed with verses by Khivan poets, supporting vibrantly painted red-and-gold wooden ceilings.
Dark, narrow, twisting corridors connect the three courtyards deliberately like a maze—both to ensure strict privacy for the harem and to disorient potential intruders.
Copper lattice grilles (panjara) and carved wooden doors screen the private rooms while filtering blinding sunlight into cool patterned shadows.
localLegends: The Tragic Fate of the First Architect: When Allakuli Khan demanded the entire palace be completed in just two years, chief architect Usto Nurmuhammad Tajikhan honestly replied that quality kiln-fired architecture and majolica could never be rushed in two years. Furious at the defiance, the Khan ordered him impaled. His successor, Usto Qalandar Khivaki, wisely promised to build as fast as humanly possible—and carefully took eight years to deliver a masterpiece while keeping his head.

Why the Khan Slept in a Yurt Inside a Palace: Local guides explain that the Qungrat rulers came from semi-nomadic steppe roots; even inside a 163-room tiled palace, the circular brick pads in the center of Ishrat-Hovli and Arz-Hovli held richly carpeted yurts because the Khans felt warmer and closer to their ancestral spirit under a felt dome in winter.

The Two Doors of Arz-Hovli: In the Court of Justice (Arz-Hovli), two separate gateways served petitioners—one for citizens entering to plead their case before the Khan, and a separate exit door used to escort those sentenced to punishment straight away from the public gaze.
visualCues: Enclosed royal courtyard surrounded by towering walls completely covered in intricate blue, white, and turquoise floral majolica tiles
Tall shaded wooden iwan porches supported by single slender carved elm columns on marble bases
Richly painted red, orange, and gold wooden coffered ceilings above the iwans
Circular raised brick platform in the middle of the paved courtyard floor for pitching a yurt

name: Kunya-Ark Fortress
architect: Founded by Arang Khan; expanded by Eltuzar Khan (1804–1806) & Allakuli Khan
locationInSite: Western edge of Ichan-Qala, directly abutting the western city wall north of Ata-Darvoza
verifiedBy: Ichan-Qala State Historical & Architectural Museum-Reserve Archive
shortDescription: Khiva's 'Old Citadel'—a fortified city-within-a-city housing the Khan's throne room, summer mosque, royal mint, prison, and Ak-Sheikh-Bobo watchtower.

localizedShortDescriptions.en: Khiva's 'Old Citadel'—a fortified city-within-a-city housing the Khan's throne room, summer mosque, royal mint, prison, and Ak-Sheikh-Bobo watchtower.
localizedShortDescriptions.uz: Xiva xonlarining 'shahar ichidagi shahar' qarorgohi — Ko'rinishxona taxt zali, Yozgi masjid, Zarbxona, Zindon va Oq-Shayx-Bobo kuzatuv minorasini o'z ichiga olgan qadimiy qal'a.
localizedShortDescriptions.ru: «Старая цитадель» Хивы — укреплённый город в городе с тронным залом Куриниш-хана, Летней мечетью, монетным двором, зинданом и башней Ак-Шейх-Бобо.
localizedShortDescriptions.ja: 玉座の間、夏のモスク、王立造幣局、牢獄、アク・シェイフ・ボボ見張り塔を備えた「城壁の中の都市」、ヒヴァの古要塞。
localizedShortDescriptions.ko: 칸의 알현실, 여름 모스크, 왕실 조폐국, 감옥, 아크 셰이크 보보 망루를 품은 '성 안의 도시' 히바의 옛 성채입니다.
localizedShortDescriptions.es: La 'Vieja Ciudadela' de Jiva: una ciudad fortificada dentro de la ciudad que alberga el salón del trono, la mezquita de verano, la casa de la moneda y la torre Ak-Sheikh-Bobo.

historicalFacts: Kunya-Ark ('Old Fortress') served as the primary fortified residence of Khiva's Khans from the late 17th century until the early 20th century, covering roughly 1.2 hectares.
The original citadel was laid out between 1686 and 1688 by Arang Khan, though much of the fortress was destroyed during the Persian invasion of Nadir Shah in 1740.

Between 1804 and 1806, Eltuzar Khan rebuilt the citadel as a self-contained royal enclave complete with its own inner walls, throne reception hall (Kurinish-Khana), summer and winter mosques, royal mint, arsenal, treasury, harem, stables, and dungeon (Zindan).

In the Kurinish-Khana reception hall sat the Khan's wooden throne clad in embossed silver sheets crafted in 1816 by master Muhammad; the original throne is preserved in Moscow's Kremlin Armory while an exact museum replica sits in the hall today.
Khiva's Royal Mint inside Kunya-Ark famously minted not only silver and gold coins (tanga and tilla) but also unique printed silk-fabric banknotes during the final years of the Khanate (1919–1920).
The Ak-Sheikh-Bobo bastion, standing on the highest earthen mound of the fortress, served both as a gunpowder storehouse and the royal observation tower overlooking all of Ichan-Qala.
architecturalDetails: The eastern entrance gateway is flanked by massive battered mud-brick watchtowers decorated with upper turquoise tile bands, opening into a fortified outer guard courtyard.

The Summer Mosque (1838) features a luminous open iwan fully tiled in deep sapphire-blue, turquoise, and white plant-scroll majolica signed by Master Ibadulla and Abdulla Jin, angled to catch cool afternoon breezes.
The Kurinish-Khana courtyard includes a double-columned ceremonial iwan facing north so the Khan sat permanently in cool shade while visiting ambassadors stood in the sunlit yard.
High crenelated paksha (rammed-clay) ramparts rise directly into Ichan-Qala's outer western defensive wall, offering a commanding 360-degree view from Ak-Sheikh-Bobo's terrace.
localLegends: Ak-Sheikh-Bobo the Hermit: Before Arang Khan built the fortress, a revered Sufi hermit named Ak-Sheikh-Bobo ('White Sheikh Grandfather') reportedly lived in meditation atop the earthen hill. Out of respect, the Khans preserved his memorial chamber inside the watchtower bastion, and locals say climbing the bastion at sunset blesses travelers with clarity and safe passage.

The Silk Money of Khiva: Elderly Khivans still tell stories of the rare Khorezm silk banknotes printed in Kunya-Ark's Mint—treasured because even after empires fell, families could wash the ink off and sew the fine silk into garments.

The Shadow of the Throne: Protocol in Kurinish-Khana was so strict that even foreign envoys had to dismount outside the main gate and bow three times before approaching the circular yurt plinth facing the silver throne.
visualCues: Massive sloped adobe/mud-brick fortress entrance flanked by two thick rounded gate towers with blue-tile mosaic bands near the top
Elevated flat earthen watchtower terrace (Ak-Sheikh-Bobo) offering panoramic sunset views over turquoise domes and minarets of Ichan-Qala
Open-air Summer Mosque courtyard covered head-to-toe in rich blue and white floral ceramic tiles
Shaded royal reception iwan (Kurinish-Khana) with carved wooden columns and a silver-covered throne alcove

name: Pahlavon Mahmud Mausoleum

localizedNames.ja: パフラワン・マフムド廟

builtYear: Original tomb 1326 · Grand Dome rebuilt 1810–1835 · Courtyard expanded 1913
architect: Master Odina Muhammad Murod; interior majolica by Mulla Nurmuhammad & Abdulla Jin
locationInSite: South-central Ichan-Qala, directly south of Juma Mosque
verifiedBy: Ichan-Qala State Historical & Architectural Museum-Reserve Archive
shortDescription: The sacred spiritual heart of Khiva and royal necropolis of its Khans, crowned by Ichan-Qala's grandest turquoise dome honoring poet, furrier, and undefeated wrestler Pahlavon Mahmud.

localizedShortDescriptions.es: El corazón espiritual de Jiva y necrópolis real de sus Khans, coronado por la mayor cúpula turquesa de Ichan-Qala en honor al poeta, peletero y luchador invicto Pahlavon Mahmud.

historicalFacts: Pahlavon Mahmud (1247–1326), known lovingly as Piryar Vali, was a celebrated Khivan furrier, Sufi philosopher, Persian-language poet (author of philosophical rubaiyat and the treatise 'Kanz al-Haqoyiq'), and undefeated master wrestler revered as Khiva's patron saint.
He was originally buried in 1326 inside his own modest workshop behind Juma Mosque, which immediately became a beloved pilgrimage shrine.
Between 1810 and 1835, Muhammad Rahim Khan I and Allakuli Khan transformed the modest tomb into a magnificent domed sanctuary and dynastic mausoleum for the Khivan royal family.

Several prominent Khiva rulers are interred in the complex alongside the saint, including Abulgazi Khan (17th-century historian-king), Anusha Khan, Muhammad Rahim Khan I, Allakuli Khan, and Isfandiyar Khan's family chambers (added in 1913).
The great turquoise-glazed dome rises 25 meters high with an internal diameter of 17.5 meters—the largest dome anywhere in Khiva—topped by a gleaming gilded copper finial (qubba).
Inside the vaulted chambers, blue-and-white Khorezmian majolica panels quote Pahlavon Mahmud's own ethical rubaiyat (quatrains) alongside Qur'anic calligraphy.
architecturalDetails: The main ceremonial hall (ziyoratkhona) beneath the monumental dome is completely sheathed from floor to vault in seamless turquoise, indigo, and white glazed majolica tiles, creating an ethereal, jewel-box interior.
Pahlavon Mahmud's actual cenotaph rests in an adjoining western side chamber (gurkhona) separated by an ornate gilded copper lattice screen, allowing pilgrims to view the richly tiled sarcophagus.
The entrance portal features deeply carved wooden doors dating to 1810 inlaid with ivory and bone motifs, leading into an intimate paved courtyard.
In the center of the tranquil courtyard stands a sacred drinking well framed by carved wooden columns and shaded verandas (qorikhona) where reciters chanted verses.
localLegends: The Legendary Match in India: According to Khorezmian tradition, Pahlavon Mahmud traveled to India where the local ruler challenged him to wrestle the empire's greatest champion. Before the match, Pahlavon Mahmud overheard the Indian wrestler's elderly mother praying tearfully that her son would not lose, as defeat meant disgrace and poverty for their family. Moved by compassion, the undefeated Khivan master deliberately allowed himself to be pinned—his only recorded loss. When the Indian king later learned of his nobility, he granted Pahlavon Mahmud any wish; Mahmud asked not for gold, but for the freedom of all Khorezmian captives held in India, asking for 'as many prisoners as can fit on one cowhide'—then as a master furrier, he sliced a single hide into a hair-thin strip wide enough to encircle every captive and bring them all home.

The Sacred Courtyard Well: Local visitors believe that drawing water from the courtyard well near the saint's shrine brings strength, humility, and blessing—and newlyweds in Khiva still visit the mausoleum on their wedding day to honor Pahlavon Mahmud.
The Poet's Motto: Elders frequently quote his famous quatrain inscribed on the tilework: 'Conquering one's own ego is harder than wrestling a hundred lions.'
visualCues: Massive glossy turquoise-green glazed bulbous dome topped with a bright golden spire finial rising above brickwork
Intimate courtyard with a traditional stone-rimmed well and carved dark wooden veranda pillars
Floor-to-ceiling luminous blue-and-white tiled vaulted interior hall with white calligraphic cartouches and majolica tombs
Ornate tiled portal framed by carved wooden doors with fine geometric inlays
